items.body:
I got on stage at HighLevel's Level Up this year.

Thousands of agency owners in one room. Most of them came to learn a new tool, a new automation, a new offer.

But the moment people kept talking about afterwards wasn't a slide.

It was the checks.

We gave away $5,000 and $10,000 to three of our SaaS Suite customers: Andy Griffith, Susie Guzman and Muneo Dongo. Real people who took the platform, built a real business on it, and showed up.

Therefore that's what I'm taking home from this week: the stage is nice, but the customer stories are the whole point. Every feature we ship is only worth what someone builds with it.

Thank you to everyone who stopped by the booth, signed the board, and grabbed a photo. And thank you to the HighLevel team for having us.

If you were there, what's the one thing you're putting into practice this month?

items.title: LinkedIn: Picture a gym owner who wants an online store.
items.body:
_Note: scenario is illustrative (demo funnel = a gym), not a real client story, swap in a real one if Andrew has it._
_Angle: what changed. Image: carousel slide 1 or the before/after funnel-steps screenshot._

Picture a gym owner who wants an online store.

Not a big one. Day passes, a few shirts, a protein tub.

Until now the answer was usually "Shopify," but that means another login, another bill, and another tool their HighLevel setup can't see.

So open their funnel instead.

One element. A cart icon, dropped into the header. HighLevel asks which sections you want to carry over, hero, gallery, testimonials, FAQ, footer, and you click Import.

Therefore their one-page funnel becomes a store: product list, product details, cart, checkout, thank-you page. Same design. Same domain. Same CRM.

It took less time than this post.

But here's the part most agencies will miss: that's not a feature. That's a product.

"I'll turn your funnel into a store this week" is something a local business will pay for. Setup fee, monthly care plan, done.

You don't need to sell all of HighLevel.

You need to sell one feature.

This is one., Andrew George · The One Feature guy · Founder, SaaSSuite

items.title: LinkedIn: Most agency owners pitch features.
items.body:
_Angle: the buyer. Image: story frame 4 or a product-list page screenshot._

Most agency owners pitch features.

But clients don't buy features. They buy "I can finally sell my thing online."

HighLevel just made that pitch easy: you can now put a full store inside an existing funnel. One click builds the product list, product details, cart, checkout and thank-you pages, using the design that's already there.

Therefore the question isn't "how do I set it up." It's "who do I sell it to?"

Here's my short list:

→ Gyms and studios: day passes, class packs, merch.
→ Coaches: workbooks, templates, a paid mini-course.
→ Local shops: gift cards and best-sellers, without a separate Shopify.
→ Restaurants and cafés: merch, sauces, catering deposits.
→ Churches and nonprofits: donations and event tickets on one page.

Every one of these already has a funnel or a website. But most of them don't have a way to take money on it.

That gap is your offer.

Pick one niche from that list. Build one demo store. Show it on the sales call.

One feature. One niche. One demo.

That's how you start a SaaS on HighLevel.

items.title: LinkedIn: I've watched hundreds of people try to sell HighLevel.
items.body:
_Angle: what this says about how to grow. Image: Andrew on stage (photo library stage-1)._

I've watched hundreds of people try to sell HighLevel.

The ones who stall all do the same thing: they sell the whole platform. CRM, calendars, automations, AI, reputation, funnels, all at once.

But the buyer hears "complicated," therefore they say "let me think about it."

The ones who grow do the opposite. They pick one feature and make it the whole offer.

Today's example: HighLevel stores can now live inside any funnel. Click an element, choose the sections, import, and a one-page funnel turns into a five-page store.

That single change is a complete offer:
• Who it's for: any local business with a funnel and something to sell.
• What it fixes: "I want to sell online but I don't want another platform."
• What you deliver: the store, live, in their branding, this week.

But one feature only works if you can explain it in one sentence.

Here's mine: "I'll turn your funnel into a store this week."

If you can't say your offer in one sentence, you're selling too much.

What's your one feature?

items.body:
**Subject options:** (A) Your client's funnel is a store now · (B) One feature, one niche, one demo · (C) The easiest "yes" in HighLevel this month
**Preview text:** One click turns a 1-page funnel into a 5-page store. Here's who'll pay for it.

---

Hey {{contact.first_name}},

Quick one today, because HighLevel shipped something that's easy to miss and easy to sell.

**Stores can now live inside an existing funnel or website.**

Before, if a client wanted to sell online inside HighLevel, you had to build a separate store from the Stores tab. Most people didn't bother. They sent the client to Shopify, therefore the client ended up with another login, another bill, and sales data that never touched the CRM.

Now it works like this:

1. Open the funnel (or website) in the builder.
2. Add any store element, a cart icon in the header is the easiest.
3. HighLevel pops up "Import theme." Tick the sections you want reused on every store page (hero, gallery, testimonials, FAQ, call to action, footer). Keep popups and fonts on.
4. Click Import.

That's it. Go back to the funnel steps and you'll see the new pages: **product list, product details, cart, checkout, thank you**, all in the design the funnel already had.

I filmed the whole thing in under three minutes. [Watch it here →] {{LINK: master reel / YouTube}}

**But here's why I'm emailing you about it.**

The setup is easy. Therefore the setup isn't worth much on its own. The *offer* is.

items.body:
I sat down with Andy Griffith, a SaaS-preneur award winner who runs 120 HighLevel SaaS customers at SoloLink.

6 things I wrote down:

1. If you're stuck at 5 to 10 accounts, keep going. Everyone with 120 started there.
2. Your first customers are your warm market. They forgive mistakes while you learn.
3. Charge less at first. "Eat a little bit of dirt." You're getting paid to learn.
4. Sell the offer before you know every step of the backend. You only need to see 200 feet ahead.
5. You can do anything, not everything. Solo breaks somewhere past 50 clients.
6. Bet on yourself. Don't fail the bet you made.

The pattern under all six: most people don't fail at SaaS. They stop early. Therefore the real skill is staying in the game long enough for the math to work.

Which one do you need to hear this week?

items.title: Newsletter: Every HighLevel agency hits the same wall.
items.body:
Every HighLevel agency hits the same wall.

You've got a platform that can do almost anything. CRM, calendars, automations, AI, reputation, funnels, courses. But when you get on a call with a local business owner and explain all of it, you can watch their eyes glaze over. Therefore you end up discounting, or bundling more, or "following up next week." The deal dies of complexity.

This week HighLevel shipped a small change that's a perfect example of the way out.


Stores can now be embedded inside an existing funnel or website. You add a single store element in the builder, a cart icon, say, and HighLevel offers to import a theme: which sections of the existing page (hero, gallery, testimonials, FAQ, footer) should carry over onto every store page. Click Import, and the funnel grows the pages a store needs: product list, product details, cart, checkout, thank you.

A one-page funnel becomes a five- or six-page store. Same design, same domain, same CRM.


On its own, this is a convenience. But put it in front of the right buyer and it becomes an offer.

A gym already has a funnel for its free-trial pass. But it sells day passes and shirts at the front desk, in cash, with no follow-up. A coach already has a lead-magnet page. But the workbook she wants to sell lives in a separate tool her CRM can't see. A café already has a website. But it has no way to sell gift cards online in December.

Each of these businesses doesn't want "HighLevel." They want *the thing they sell, sold online, this week.* Therefore the pitch writes itself: "I'll turn your funnel into a store."

items.title: LinkedIn: The call goes great. They nod. They say "we're ready."
items.body:
_From Get Real ep. 3 "Positive to Payment"._

The call goes great. They nod. They say "we're ready."

Then nothing. Weeks of silence.

I had this happen so often in my first years of sales that I wrote a document about it. I called it Positive to Payment.

Here's the short version. People pay you when three things are true:

1. They understand they have a problem.
2. They trust you to fix it.
3. They have a way to pay you, right now.

Most deals die on number three. Therefore the payment link should be ready before the call starts, not "I'll send it over."

A positive reaction means nothing until it turns into a payment.

items.title: LinkedIn: A band director told me something years ago that still runs my sales p…
items.body:
A band director told me something years ago that still runs my sales process.

"You have to make deposits in people before you can make a withdrawal."

Every relationship has a give-to-ask ratio. But most people in sales ask too soon. They try to withdraw from an account they never paid into.

I call it perceived relationship equity. How much you've given before you ask.

Therefore the sales process is really a question: how fast can this person come to like and trust me?

Give value first. Make them feel heard. Explain exactly how you'd solve the problem.

Then ask.

items.title: LinkedIn: "If closing feels high pressure, you haven't sold them enough yet."
items.body:
"If closing feels high pressure, you haven't sold them enough yet."

When someone's already in, they understand the problem, they trust you, they're happy, asking for payment isn't pressure. It's the next step.

So I do it live. "Here's the link. Let's get it taken care of." Then I stay on the call while they pay.

But the sale doesn't end there. Buyers get remorse. Therefore what you do in the first hour after they pay matters as much as the call itself: a thank-you, something extra, a reason to feel good about the decision.

Positive → payment → reinforcement. Skip the last step and you'll feel it in refunds.

items.title: LinkedIn: Blake Coker built an agency for midsize banks. Not roofers, not dentists. Banks.
items.body:
Blake Coker built an agency for midsize banks. Not roofers, not dentists. Banks.

What stood out from our conversation:

1. His niche came from his resume. He'd built software for banks for years.
2. His first real bank client came from one referral: "go talk to our marketing manager."
3. He walked into that first meeting with a notepad and kept his mouth shut.
4. He didn't pitch the whole marketing job. He filled the gap their team couldn't.
5. Forget speed to lead. Speed to support is what keeps clients.
6. Offer one thing. Then find your groove.

None of that is a growth hack. But all of it compounds. Therefore if you're starting an agency, start with who already trusts you and what you already know.

**Preview text:** Most "yes" calls die on one missing step.

---

Hey {{contact.first_name}},

Picture the call. They're nodding, they like you, they say "we're ready, we just need a bit of time."

Then weeks go by and the deal fizzles out.

I lived in that loop when I started selling, so I wrote myself a document called **Positive to Payment**. I talked through it on the latest episode of Get Real. Here's the short version.

**People pay you when three things are true:**
1. **They understand they have a problem.** Ask questions until they say it out loud.
2. **They trust you to fix it.** "We can fix that" isn't enough. Show exactly how. That's why founders often outsell hired reps: they built the solution.
3. **They have a way to pay you right now.** A payment link or invoice ready before the call ends.

But even with all three, you need **commitment**: small actions they take with you that they don't take with anyone else (a lead magnet, a video, replying to your emails). If you're on HighLevel, engagement scoring on your contacts shows you who's actually leaning in.

Then **get paid live.** Send the link and stay on the call. If that feels like pressure, you haven't sold them enough yet.

And after they pay, **reinforce the decision.** A thank-you, something extra. Buyer's remorse is real.

Positive reactions mean nothing until they turn into payment.

🎧 Full episode: {{LINK: Get Real ep. 3}}

items.title: Newsletter: Every salesperson has a graveyard of great calls.
items.body:
Every salesperson has a graveyard of great calls.

The prospect laughed at your jokes. They agreed with everything. They said "we're ready." But then they needed time to think, and time turned into silence.

I spent my first years of sales in that graveyard, so I wrote myself a rule book. I called it Positive to Payment, and I recently walked through it on my podcast.

Every relationship has a give-to-ask ratio. Most people ask too soon, therefore the ask feels like a withdrawal from an account that was never funded. I call the balance perceived relationship equity. Your job on a first call isn't to pitch. It's to make deposits: be useful, listen, make them feel understood.

People pay when they (1) understand they have a problem, (2) trust you to fix it, and (3) have a way to pay you. The second one is where transparency wins. "We can fix your website" means nothing. "Here's how we'll fix it, and who does what" means everything. The third one sounds obvious, but it's where most "yes" calls die: the payment link isn't ready.

The more someone invests in the relationship, signing up for your lead magnet, watching your video, replying to your emails, the more likely they are to pay. That's why I like engagement scores: they turn "they seemed interested" into a number.

If they're in, send the link and stay with them while they pay. If that feels high pressure, you skipped a step. And after they pay, reinforce the decision. What you do in the hour after the sale protects the sale.

A positive reaction is a feeling. A payment is a decision. Build the bridge between them on pu

items.title: LinkedIn: Most HighLevel clients don't churn because the software is bad.
items.body:
Most HighLevel clients don't churn because the software is bad.

They churn because they log in, see 20 tabs, and never come back.

But HighLevel's new navigation lets you fix that per client. Hide sections. Reorder tabs. Add one-click links to the three screens they actually use. Save it as a layout and apply it to other sub-accounts.

Therefore you can sell something most agencies can't: a HighLevel that looks like it was built for one industry.

Who pays for that?

→ Agencies with 10+ sub-accounts in one niche (med spas, roofers, gyms) who are tired of "where do I find…" tickets.
→ SaaS builders selling a white-label CRM who need it to feel simple on day one.
→ Coaches and consultants who give clients a portal and want only 4 tabs visible.

The setup takes minutes. But the outcome, fewer support tickets, clients who actually log in, is what they're paying for.

One feature. One niche. One layout.

items.title: LinkedIn: Where do your first SaaS customers come from?
items.body:
Where do your first SaaS customers come from?

Andy Griffith (SoloLink) says: your warm market.

People who already trust you because of who you are and the work you've done. You tell them "I'm building something" and a few will take a chance or send a referral.

But the part I liked most was why. Warm customers are patient. You will make mistakes in the first months. They forgive them.

Therefore don't burn cold traffic on a product that isn't ready. Learn on the people who'll give you grace. Then scale.

items.title: LinkedIn: "HighLevel is too complicated" is the most common objection I hear.
items.body:
_Image: Andrew on stage (photo library stage-2)._

"HighLevel is too complicated" is the most common objection I hear.

For years the honest answer was "yes, it is." You could train clients, record Looms, build help docs. But they still logged into a screen with every feature on it.

The new HighLevel UI changes the answer.

You can now decide what each client sees. Hide the sections they'll never use, pin the ones they need, and save that as a layout you apply across sub-accounts.

Therefore "too complicated" becomes a design choice you control.

But here's the lesson I'd take from it, beyond the feature: simplicity is the product.

Clients don't pay for more features. They pay for fewer decisions.

That's the whole idea behind SaaSSuite, one place for your clients to onboard, learn and get support. The new layouts are the same idea inside HighLevel itself.

What would you hide first?

Open any funnel or website, add a store element like a cart icon, and HighLevel asks which sections you want to reuse. Click import and it builds the product list, product details, cart, checkout and thank-you pages in the same design.

One page becomes a six-page store.

That matters because most local businesses already have a funnel but no way to sell products on it: gyms with merch, coaches with templates, cafes with gift cards.

Therefore every funnel you've built is now an upsell conversation.

Hey {{contact.first_name}},

If you've ever had a client say "I can't find anything in here," this one's for you.

HighLevel rolled out a new UI you can turn on per sub-account. Most of it is navigation: the account switcher moved to a collapsed left nav, all the AI tools now sit under one AI tab, and the old row of buttons along the top became a dropdown.

Clients don't leave HighLevel because it can't do enough. They leave because it does too much, and they get lost. Therefore the agency that shows up with a clean, niche-specific layout wins the "this is easy" moment on day one.

items.title: Newsletter: There's a moment every HighLevel agency knows. The client logs in for …
items.body:
There's a moment every HighLevel agency knows. The client logs in for the first time, looks at the screen, and goes quiet.

They see twenty tabs. Pipelines, workflows, reputation, memberships, affiliate manager, AI studio. They came for a calendar and an inbox, but now they're looking at a cockpit. Therefore they close the tab and send you a text instead.

HighLevel's new UI is the first time the platform itself gives you a real fix.

Inside the new interface, the left-hand navigation has an Edit button. You can reorder tabs, hide whole sections, add quick links to the screens a client actually uses, rename categories and change icons. Then you save that layout and apply it to other sub-accounts.

You decide what your client sees.

"Too complicated" has always been HighLevel's biggest objection. You couldn't change the software, so you added training: Looms, help docs, onboarding calls. All useful. But the screen stayed the same.

Now the screen can change. A med spa gets Conversations, Calendar, Contacts and Reviews. A roofer gets Opportunities and the inbox. Nobody gets Affiliate Manager unless they asked for it.

- **The feature:** custom navigation layouts.
- **Who pays:** agencies with many clients in one niche, white-label SaaS builders, consultants with client portals.
- **What it sells:** "HighLevel, built for your industry." Fewer support tickets. Clients who log in.
- **How to deliver:** design one layout per niche, save it, apply it everywhere.

But a clean menu is only the first step. Clients still need to be onboarded, taught and supported. That's what I built

items.title: Basic agencies get squeezed · LinkedIn
items.body:
I think basic marketing agencies have 6 to 12 months.

Not because they're bad. Because their clients are about to learn a new skill: using AI to use software.

If all you do is set up a CRM, build a website and manage it, the client will soon ask a fair question: why wouldn't I just ask Claude, or go to HighLevel directly?

But that doesn't mean agencies die. It means the job changes.

Therefore I'd focus on two things:

1. AI competency. The gap between what you can build with AI and what your client knows is your margin. Keep it wide.
2. Wrap it simpler. Most people will never go to HighLevel directly because it feels too complicated. Make it simple for them. That's the product.

The agencies that win won't sell software. They'll sell the gap.

items.title: Sell the AI setup, not the tool · LinkedIn
items.body:
Walk into a local restaurant and ask how they post on Facebook.

"Manually. When I remember."

You could show them an AI system that does it. You could even log them into one. But they'd use it for a week and stop.

Not because it's hard. Because they don't know what it can do.

That's the real gap. Not "how to use AI." What AI can take off their plate. Anything they do on a screen, an agent can probably handle.

And the setup won't become one-click anytime soon. Security, logins and permissions keep it complicated.

Therefore the opportunity is: build the AI setup for one kind of business, teach them what it can do, give them a simple chat to run it, and duplicate it.

One system. One niche. Then the next client.

items.title: 3 starter automations · LinkedIn
items.body:
Before a new client gets their HighLevel login, I set up three automations.

1. Missed call text-back. A form fill or missed call gets a text in under 60 seconds. Therefore no lead dies waiting.

2. Review requests. 48 hours after service, an SMS with the Google review link. No reply in three days, a follow-up email. My clients average a full star improvement within 90 days.

3. Appointment reminders. Confirmed 24 hours out, reminded one hour before. No-shows drop close to zero.

But the point isn't the automations. It's that these three replace tools most clients already pay for.

Make sure all three run before you hand over the keys.

items.title: Email warm-up · LinkedIn
items.body:
People launch their first HighLevel broadcast cold, and half of it lands in spam.

Then they blame the copy.

But it's not the copy. It's the sender reputation.

HighLevel has email warm-up built in. It slowly builds your reputation by trading low-volume, natural emails with other accounts before your real campaigns go out. Dedicated warm-up tools charge $15–$30 a month for this.

Sub-account settings → Email Services → warm-up toggle.

Therefore the rule is simple: turn it on at least two weeks before your first broadcast.

items.title: Voice AI booking · LinkedIn
items.body:
A lead calls your client's business at 11 PM on a Saturday.

Nobody's there. But the call still gets answered.

HighLevel's Voice AI picks up, has a real conversation, qualifies the caller and books them straight into the calendar based on actual availability. Then it sends the confirmation.

Standalone AI phone agents run $100–$500 a month.

But I'll be real: setup matters. You configure the persona, the script and the calendar connection. It doesn't just switch on.

Therefore the offer isn't "AI." It's "your phone books appointments 24/7." Home services, medical, anything appointment-based.

Here's one feature you can sell.

items.title: Manual Actions · LinkedIn
items.body:
Everyone wants to automate everything.

But the deals that close usually need one human moment.

HighLevel's Manual Actions handle exactly that. Inside any workflow, add a step that creates a task for a specific team member: "Call and check in on the proposal." "Confirm the appointment." "Review this intake form." It lands in their queue at the right time.

It's your automation raising its hand and saying: this one needs a person.

Therefore your workflows don't have to do everything. They handle 90% of the process and hand the right 10% to the right person.

Add at least one manual action checkpoint to every pipeline stage.

Andy on the trap of doing it all yourself. Works at 5-10 customers. At 50, 60, 100 plus? Impossible.

#agencyowner #entrepreneur #saas #delegation
items.notes: Guest: Andy, SoloLink (SaaS Gold winner, ~120 accounts) — confirm name/brand spelling.
items.transcript: The saying that I've heard is, I can do anything, but I can't do everything. I know I did it. I think a lot of us get stuck in that kind of trap of trying to do everything. And it works when you get started. Like it does. Like there's nothing wrong with that when you get started. Like you can run an agency with your first five, 10 customers and do it all yourself. Easy. Easy. But yeah, well, I mean, once you're getting to 50, 60, 100 plus customers, yeah, it's impossible.

items.title: Offer one thing. Then find your groove.
items.make: Render V5 (Split question) of pod2-09: tools/formats.py
items.speaker: Blake
items.hook_q: One piece of advice for new agency owners?
items.body:
Blake's advice for new agency owners: don't sit back and wait.

Talk to people. Go to events. He went to BNI and Chamber of Commerce meetings when he started.

#gohighlevel #agencyowner #networking #smallbusiness
items.transcript: I would say probably don't sit back and wait. If you're on the fence and you really wanna get out there, just start talking to people. I mean, I know you've talked about it, I mean, but get involved, go to events. When I first started, I went to B &I meetings. I went to Chamber of Commerce meetings and just have confidence in yourself. And find one thing that you can offer someone and don't try to do too much. There's so much out there. I think if you can make a great living or you can really get a great start just by starting off offering one thing.

items.title: Started an agency in high school. Felt like an outcast.

items.speaker: McKinley
items.hook_q: Is building a business lonely?
items.hook_plain: Agency at 16. Zero friends who got it.
items.body:
Started an agency in high school. Most of the friend group didn't get it.

McKinley on how lonely building a business can feel when your friends aren't into business, marketing or content.

If that's you, you're not the only one.

#entrepreneur #youngentrepreneur #agencyowner #gohighlevel
items.transcript: I think I started my agency back in high school and was very much, I wouldn't say made fun of, but a little bit of an outcast when it comes to your typical friend group. They're not into business, they're not into marketing, they don't really do content creation or anything like that. It's definitely been kind of a lonely route in some portions of business.

items.title: Show me your 3 friends, I'll show you your future
items.make: Render V6 (Serious crop) of pod3-03: tools/formats.py
items.speaker: Ohaji
items.hook_q: Are your friends holding you back?
items.body:
Show me your 3 friends and I'll show you where you're going in life.

Ohaji from our HighLevel interns on watching others get clients while he had none. Your ecosystem matters.

#gohighlevel #mindset #entrepreneur #success
items.transcript: Even during the internship, we went through periods this time, me specifically, where it's just hard. It's hard, I was feeling, seeing people get clients, and I'm like, well, where are my clients? I'm doing everything right, supposedly. But one thing that really killed me growing up was obviously the people around me. Your ecosystem, you are who you're around. You show me your three friends, and I'll show you where you're going in life.

items.title: Charge less at first. You're getting paid to learn.
items.make: Render V6 (Serious crop) of pod1-05: tools/formats.py
items.speaker: Andy
items.hook_q: Should you charge less when you're starting out?
items.body:
Charging less at first? You're getting paid to learn.

Andy says you have to eat a little dirt in the beginning. Go free or go low.
Then earn the right to charge what you're worth.

#agencyowner #saas #entrepreneur #pricing
items.notes: Guest: Andy, SoloLink (SaaS Gold winner, ~120 accounts) — confirm name/brand spelling.
items.transcript: you may want to charge higher ticket prices for your services, but in the beginning, you have to eat a little bit of dirt, in my opinion, and maybe you have to go free or go low, but you're getting paid to learn. And that's, in my mind's eye, think of it as like, you know you want to do this anyways. If you can even offer it at a lower price than you normally would, you're getting paid to learn how to do it. And then you can earn the right privilege to charge what is the right amount for you and your services.

items.title: Forget speed to lead. Speed to support.
items.make: Render V6 (Serious crop) of pod2-07: tools/formats.py
items.speaker: Blake
items.hook_q: Is slow support killing your agency?
items.hook_plain: Speed to support > speed to lead
items.body:
Everyone talks about speed to lead. Blake cares about speed to support.

Task Engine has a ticket button right in the app, so people get help fast when they get stuck.

#gohighlevel #saas #customersupport #agencyowner
items.transcript: We actually have a direct ticket system built inside the app as well. So when people are using task engine and they run into something, they can literally click a button, submit a ticket to our team, and then we can turn around and respond to that. And I think it's a big necessity is speed. Everybody talks about speed to lead and speed, but I think about speed to support. I think that when people get caught up, they want an answer quick.

items.title: If you're gonna fail, fail forward
items.make: Render V6 (Serious crop) of pod3-10: tools/formats.py
items.speaker: Ty
items.hook_q: What's the right way to fail?
items.body:
If you're gonna fail, fail forward.

Ty's advice from my podcast with HighLevel's 2026 interns: stumble a little further than you did yesterday.

#gohighlevel #entrepreneur #mindset #agencyowner
items.transcript: if you're gonna fail, fail forward, if you're gonna fall, fall forward, always try to, you know, stumble a little bit further than what you were yesterday. Yeah. And I think that's one of the things the internship really did, you know, put instill in us. Resilience and determination was a huge takeaway.

items.title: Stretch it: fluff. Shrink it: you cut gold.
items.make: Render V6 (Serious crop) of pod1-13: tools/formats.py
items.speaker: Andy
items.hook_q: How long should your videos be?
items.body:
Stretch it and you add fluff. Shrink it and you cut gold.

Andy on video length: know what you're going to say, and don't force it to be an hour.

#contentcreator #youtube #contentstrategy #entrepreneur
items.notes: Guest: Andy, SoloLink (SaaS Gold winner, ~120 accounts) — confirm name/brand spelling.
items.transcript: if you're trying to stretch information, you're gonna put fluff in. If you're trying to shrink information, you're probably gonna cut gold out. Know what you're gonna talk about, but also don't feel like it has to be an hour long thing. That can be a YouTube video. And then you've got, we have tools out there that you can then turn that into shorts and clips and even pull the audio from it to find quotes. And then you can find images of you and put quotes.
